record.paper_title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model
record.original_question: Can apparent-magnitude-versus-distance and angular-size-versus-redshift observations distinguish static and expanding cosmologies when the analysis depends on uncertain luminosity evolution and on identifying standard candles or standard rods whose intrinsic size, mass, and brightness do not vary with redshift except according to a known evolutionary scheme?

evidence.quote: This disagreement could however be solved by an increase of luminosity at higher redshift due to the evolution of galaxies (which is a possible observational result pointed out from deep infrared FIRES and HST data[72]), so the uncertainties in the luminosity evolution do not allow this to be a proof against expansion.

However, the main problem of such a type of test is the identification of the “standard stick” for which one knows reliably its non-variation with redshift, or its variation with a well-known evolutionary scheme so we must be cautious too to interpret the results of this test as a definitive proof of a particular cosmological model, in this case the static Universe.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider two classes of cosmological models for the large-scale universe:

(A) Expanding models, in which the observed redshift z of a distant source arises from cosmological expansion, so that the luminosity distance is d_L(z) = (1+z) d_M(z) and the angular-size distance is d_A(z) = d_M(z)/(1+z), where d_M(z) is the transverse comoving distance determined by a Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker metric.

(B) Static models, in which redshift arises from some non-expansion mechanism (e.g. a tired-light hypothesis), and luminosity distance and angular-size distance obey a different relation, typically d_L^stat(z) = d(z)(1+z)^{1/2} and d_A^stat(z) = d(z), for some monotonic distance–redshift relation d(z).

Suppose one performs cosmological tests using:
 (i) the apparent-magnitude–redshift (Hubble) relation m(z) for a population of sources of intrinsic absolute magnitude M(z) = M_0 + ΔM_evol(z), and
 (ii) the angular-size–redshift relation θ(z) for a population of objects of intrinsic linear size L(z) = L_0 + ΔL_evol(z),
where ΔM_evol(z) and ΔL_evol(z) are evolutionary corrections that are not known a priori but must be modeled.

Question: Under what precise hypotheses on the admissible class of evolutionary corrections {ΔM_evol(z), ΔL_evol(z)} is it possible, given perfect observational data m(z) and θ(z), to discriminate uniquely between the expanding class (A) and the static class (B)? Equivalently, characterize when the Hubble diagram and the angular-size–redshift relation, jointly, can be made consistent with both classes by suitable choices of standard-candle and standard-rod evolution, so that no decisive test between expansion and a static universe is possible from these two relations alone.
artifact.status_search_result: The question concerns a long-standing methodological issue in observational cosmology: whether classical cosmological tests (Hubble diagram, angular-size–redshift) can definitively rule out static (e.g. tired-light) cosmologies once luminosity and size evolution are admitted. The literature (e.g. Lopez-Corredoira's reviews, surface-brightness Tolman tests by Lubin & Sandage, and subsequent work) reports that, while expansion is strongly favored within ΛCDM, the discriminating power of these specific tests remains limited by uncertain evolutionary corrections, and the methodological question is treated as still open in revisionist/critical reviews up through the mid-2020s.

status_evidence.title: Tests and problems of the standard model in Cosmology (Lopez-Corredoira)
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews how Hubble diagram and angular-size tests are affected by evolutionary corrections, concluding that they do not give a definitive proof against static cosmologies.
status_evidence.claim: Methodological ambiguity due to evolution remains unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Lubin & Sandage, Tolman surface-brightness test
status_evidence.snippet: Surface-brightness test favors expansion only after assuming a luminosity-evolution model from population synthesis.
status_evidence.claim: Discrimination depends sensitively on assumed evolution.
